summary: Gives generic rules for forwarding 6LoWPAN fragments across a multi-hop route-over network. Forwarding fragments can improve end-to-end latency and reliability and reduce buffer needs on intermediate nodes. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a big message is cut into pieces, a node in the middle can pass each piece along right away instead of waiting to collect all of them. This document gives rules for doing that.

questions: what is a virtual reassembly buffer
what are the caveats of vrb
subtitle: Let nodes in a low-power mesh pass 6LoWPAN fragments along at once instead of reassembling the whole packet at every hop.

tldr.problem: In a route-over 6LoWPAN network, each intermediate node reassembles a fragmented packet, routes it, and fragments it again. That adds latency at every hop and ties up scarce memory.
tldr.mechanism: The routing decision is made on the first fragment, which carries the IPv6 header. The node stores a little state and forwards every later fragment along the same path without reassembling, swapping in its own Datagram_Tag.
tldr.outcome: Latency and buffer needs drop, but the approach has caveats: no recovery of a single missing fragment, one fixed path per datagram, and a VRB table that can fill up. RFC 8931 defines a technique that adds end-to-end fragment recovery.

facts.label: VRB footprint versus a full buffer

today: RFC 8930 is a Proposed Standard, published in November 2020, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. RFC 8931 is named in the text as a 6LFF technique that adds end-to-end fragment recovery.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The original 6LoWPAN fragmentation in RFC 4944 was defined for use over a single Layer 3 hop. In a route-over 6LoWPAN network, an IP packet is expected to be reassembled at each intermediate hop, uncompressed, pushed to Layer 3 to be routed, and then compressed and fragmented again.

This document introduces an alternative called 6LoWPAN Fragment Forwarding (6LFF). An intermediate node forwards a fragment without reassembling it if the next hop is a similar 6LoWPAN link. The first fragment is forwarded immediately, and the node stores state so the following fragments can take the same path.

The RFC gives a generic overview of 6LFF, its advantages and caveats, and one particular technique, the Virtual Reassembly Buffer (VRB), that keeps the message formats of RFC 4944. It also recommends an inter-frame gap between fragments to avoid the most typical problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally every helper along the way waits to collect the whole message before passing it on. This document lets helpers pass pieces along right away.

sections.title: How 6LoWPAN Fragmentation Works
sections.content:
Node A compresses an IPv6 packet using the mechanism of RFC 6282. If the result does not fit in one link-layer frame, A's 6LoWPAN sub-layer cuts it into fragments and sends each as a separate frame to node B. B reassembles them, inflates the compressed header back to a full IPv6 header, and hands the packet to its IPv6 layer.

Every fragment carries a 16-bit Datagram_Tag that says which packet it belongs to. B indexes its reassembly buffer by A's link-layer address and that tag, so A must use the same link-layer address for all fragments of one datagram. The buffer also holds the pieces received so far, a record of which fragments arrived, the Datagram_Size and a timer that discards a partial packet after a timeout.

Because each fragment states the packet length, B can allocate a full buffer even if the first fragment it sees is not the first fragment sent. The result is per-hop fragmentation and reassembly: the packet is fully reassembled and then fragmented again at every hop.
sections.plainLanguage: A long letter is cut into numbered pages, each stamped with the same letter ID. The receiver keeps a folder for that ID and waits until every page has arrived.

sections.title: Why Per-Hop Reassembly Hurts
sections.content:
The RFC names two limitations. The first is latency: a node must wait for all fragments before it can re-form the IPv6 packet and forward it, and this repeats at every hop.

The second is memory and reliability. Constrained nodes have limited memory. Assuming a reassembly buffer for a 6LoWPAN MTU of 1280 bytes, typical nodes only have enough memory for 1-3 reassembly buffers.

In the RFC's example, nodes A, B, C and D all send through node E, which can hold only 3 reassembly buffers. If A, B and C send fragmented packets at the same time, all three buffers are used, so when D also sends one, E has to drop a packet and end-to-end reliability suffers.
sections.plainLanguage: If a helper must wait for every page and only has room for three folders, a fourth letter has nowhere to go and gets thrown away.

sections.title: Forwarding Fragments
sections.content:
A 6LFF node makes the routing decision on the first fragment, which always carries the destination IPv6 address. On receiving a first fragment, a forwarding node MUST attempt to create state and forward the fragment. This is atomic: if the first fragment cannot be forwarded, the state MUST be removed.

Since a Datagram_Tag is tied to the source link-layer address, the forwarder MUST assign a new Datagram_Tag from its own namespace for the next hop and rewrite the fragment header of every fragment. For a later fragment, it MUST look up state by source link-layer address and Datagram_Tag. With no state the fragment MUST be dropped, otherwise it is forwarded using the stored information.

The first fragment MUST always be sent first. A sender should do all its retries on the first fragment before sending the rest, and abort the datagram and release its state if the first fragment fails. The stored state also has a timer that should be longer than the one covering reassembly at the receiving endpoint.

Consecutive fragments of one datagram MUST be separated by an inter-frame gap. On a half-duplex radio, a node forwarding one fragment can miss the next one from the previous hop, and hidden-terminal interference can occur. The gap lets a fragment move beyond the next hop and the interference domain before the next one shows up, and interleaving packets or fragments sent via different next-hop routers can achieve it.
sections.plainLanguage: The first page tells the helper where the letter is going, so the helper remembers the route and sends later pages the same way. The helper also waits a moment between pages so they do not bump into each other.

sections.title: The Virtual Reassembly Buffer
sections.content:
The VRB is a particular 6LFF that can be implemented without changing RFC 4944. Nodes do not wait for the last fragment before forwarding, which reduces end-to-end latency. The memory footprint is only the VRB table, which reduces the drop probability significantly.

A table entry holds at minimum the link-layer addresses of the predecessor and successor, the Datagram_Tag used by the predecessor and the local tag swapped in. It may also keep a few octets of the last fragment that did not fit in the MTU. The RFC says this is 2 orders of magnitude smaller than a 1280-byte reassembly buffer per packet.

The RFC lists three caveats:

  • Non-zero drop probability: the VRB table is finite, so if a node must forward more packets at once than it has entries, packets are dropped.
  • No fragment recovery: there is no way to ask for a single missing fragment, so a drop means resending the whole packet.
  • No per-fragment routing: all fragments follow the first fragment's path, because only the first carries the IP header.

Whether these are acceptable depends on the link layer and the application. RFC 8931 is given as an example of a 6LFF technique that allows end-to-end fragment recovery between the endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a big folder per letter, the helper keeps a tiny note saying where each letter came from and where it is going. The notes are small, but there is still only room for so many.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
6LoWPAN operations depend on link-layer security that keeps out rogue access, and secure joining protects against network outsiders. Beyond that, the RFC relates the threats in RFC 8900 to 6LoWPAN fragments:

  • Overlapping fragments: a firewall SHOULD NOT forward fragments but recompose the packet, check it, and refragment if needed. It MUST drop the whole packet if overlapping fragments carry different data at the same offset.
  • Resource exhaustion: an attacker can send many bogus first fragments to fill the VRB table. An implementation MUST keep the number of VRBs within capacity and destroy old ones on timeout.
  • Predictable identifiers: the Datagram_Tag SHOULD be assigned pseudorandomly.
  • NIDS evasion: this makes little sense here because the intruder would already be inside the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors could flood the helper with fake first pages to use up its notes. So the helper must cap how many notes it keeps and throw old ones away.
